drapeaux.note: Phrase “articulated on the exterior” copied from the Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report, Seagram Building (LP-1664, 1989), seen in the text of the PDF https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/1664.pdf (“The juxtaposition of the structural members, articulated on the exterior by extruded bronze, with the transparent glass surfaces of the elegant curtain wall creates the balance between solid and void which typifies International style design.”). The report's “applied to represent structural intent” and the 520-foot frame, concrete and gypsum-block details were also checked there.

titre: Seagram Building: The Bronze I-Beams on the Facade Are Not the Structure
accroche: The bronze uprights of the Seagram Building, completed in 1958, look like columns. The designation report says they are applied to represent the structure.
contenu_vulgarise:
At 375 Park Avenue in New York, the Seagram Building is one of the emblems of modern architecture: a 38-story tower built from 1956 to 1958, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe with Philip Johnson. Its facade is rhythmically marked by long bronze verticals that rise without interruption, and that the eye reads as the uprights carrying the building. The designation report says, however, that they are applied to represent the structure.

## What the Designation Report Says

The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the building a landmark in 1989 and describes its construction precisely. The tower is marked by extruded bronze I-beams, 4.5 by 6 inches, or about 11 by 15 centimeters, which are continuous vertical elements, applied, the commission writes, to represent the structural intent and to cast shadow on the surface.

The actual frame is elsewhere. It is a 520-foot steel skeleton, the tallest office frame erected up to then with high-strength bolts, with vertical truss bracing. The exterior columns and all the beams are encased in concrete, the interior columns protected by gypsum blocks. Between this skeleton and the street, the cladding consists of 153,000 square feet of bronze and 122,000 square feet of pinkish-gray tinted glass.

## Why the Steel Is Hidden

The designation report does not say why the steel is encased. According to the Wikipedia article on the building, American regulations of the time required structural steel to be fire-protected, for example by concrete. The same article specifies that the bronze uprights serve only an aesthetic function.

The designation report says both things at once. It describes the structural elements as “articulated on the exterior” by extruded bronze, balanced against the glass surfaces, which it says creates the contrast between solid and void that is characteristic of the International Style. And it specifies that the I-beams are applied to represent the structural intent. The structure is thus evoked, not shown.

## What the Facade Says About the Building

What the passerby sees is a polished image of the structure, set in front of the real structure that cannot be seen. According to the Wikipedia article, the Seagram is the first office building in the world to use extruded bronze on its facade.

The facade then raises a question: what do we expect of it, that it tell how the building stands up, or how we want it to be seen?

repere.texte: According to the 1989 designation report of the Landmarks Preservation Commission, the exterior columns and all the beams of the Seagram Building's steel frame are encased in concrete, and its 4.5-by-6-inch bronze I-beams are applied to represent the structural intent.
repere.source: Landmarks Preservation Commission (New York), Seagram Building, LP-1664, October 3, 1989

carte.punch: At the Seagram Building, bronze I-beams are applied to represent the structure.
carte.idee: On the facade of the Seagram Building (New York, 1958), long bronze I-beams look like columns. The 1989 designation report says they are applied to represent the structure: the real frame is steel, with exterior columns and beams encased in concrete.

quiz.question: What does the 1989 designation report say about the Seagram Building's bronze I-beams?
choix: That they carry the building, whose steel frame remains visible behind the glazing of the facade
That they are applied to represent the structural intent, in front of exterior columns and beams encased in concrete
That they were added after 1958 to strengthen the tower against wind and tremors
That they form the upper part of a frame made entirely of solid bronze
quiz.explication: The commission describes continuous I-beams, applied to represent the structural intent, in front of a steel frame whose exterior columns and beams are encased in concrete (the interior columns are protected by gypsum blocks). The other options give them a load-bearing role or a date that the report does not mention.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why is the steel of the Seagram Building's frame not visible on the facade?
choix: Its exterior columns and beams are encased in concrete, which Wikipedia links to fire protection
It was painted bronze to imitate the facade's I-beams exactly
The frame is made entirely of reinforced concrete, with no steel in the columns
The columns were moved to the center of the building after construction ended
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The designation report describes exterior columns and beams encased in concrete; according to Wikipedia, regulations required structural steel to be fire-protected. The report mentions neither painted steel, nor a frame without steel, nor relocated columns.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Wikipedia article on the Seagram Building claim about the bronze on its facade?
choix: That bronze was used there for the first time in France
That bronze was used to make the main beams
That it is the first office building in the world to use extruded bronze on its facade
That the bronze was replaced with aluminum as early as 1960
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Wikipedia article reports that the Seagram is the first office building in the world to use extruded bronze on its facade. Bronze is not used for the main beams there, and nothing in it suggests a replacement with aluminum.
